# Re: Statement of special tax benefits to the Company and its shareholders under the direct and indirect tax laws

This Statement is issued in accordance with the Engagement Letter dated January 21, 2026, read with and as amended by way of a letter dated June 04, 2026.

We, Kirtane &#x26; Pandit LLP, Chartered Accountants, statutory auditors of the Company, have received a request from the Company to report the possible special tax benefits, available to the Company, and its shareholders under the direct and indirect tax laws presently in force in India, as on the date of this report. This is for the limited purpose of the red herring prospectus (“RHP”) which the Company intends to file with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”), BSE Limited (“BSE”), National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”) along with any relevant stock exchange(s) where the Equity Shares of the Company are proposed to be listed (the “Stock Exchanges”) and any other documents or materials in relation to the Offer (collectively, the “Offer Documents”).

The preparation of the statement (“Statement”) attached (“Annexure I”) to this report is the responsibility of the management of the Company.

We hereby report that the enclosed Annexure I provides a statement of the possible special tax benefits available to the Company and its shareholders under direct and indirect tax laws, including the Income Tax Act, 2025, as amended by the Finance Act 2026, i.e., applicable for the tax year 2026-2027, the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, the Union Territory Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, respective State Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (collectively the “GST Act”), the Customs Act, 1962 (“Customs Act”) and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (“Tariff Act”) each read with the relevant rules, circulars, and notifications issued thereunder and each as amended from time to time, as applicable and in force as at the date of this report (collectively, the “Tax Laws”).

Several of these benefits are dependent on the Company and/or its shareholders, as the case may be, fulfilling the conditions prescribed under the relevant provisions of the Tax Laws. Hence, the ability of the Company and/or its shareholders to derive the possible special tax benefits is dependent upon their fulfilling such conditions, if any, which based on business imperatives the Company and/or its shareholders face in the future, the Company and/or its shareholders may or may not choose to fulfil.

While the term ‘special tax benefit’ has not been defined in the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the benefits discussed in the enclosed Statement cover only the possible special tax benefits available to the Company and its shareholders and do not cover any general tax benefits (under both direct and indirect tax laws) available to them. The benefits discussed in the enclosed Statement are not exhaustive. Any benefits under the Tax Laws other than those specified in the Statement are considered to be general tax benefits and therefore not covered within the ambit of the Statement.

In respect of shareholders, the enclosed Statement contains only those tax benefits which accrue to the shareholders of the Company by virtue of them being shareholders as on the date of this report. Further in respect of non-residents shareholders, the tax rates and the consequent taxation shall be further subject to any benefits available under the applicable double taxation avoidance agreement, if any, between India and the country in which the non-resident shareholder has fiscal domicile.

The Statement is only intended to provide general information to the investors and is neither designed nor intended to be a substitute for professional tax advice. In view of the individual nature of the tax consequences and changing tax laws, each investor is advised to consult his or her own tax consultant with respect to the specific tax implications arising out of their participation in the Offer.

Annexure 1
# STATEMENT OF SPECIAL TAX BENEFITS AVAILABLE TO SBI FUNDS MANAGEMENT LIMITED AND ITS SHAREHOLDERS UNDER THE APPLICABLE DIRECT TAX LAWS IN INDIA

Outlined below are the benefits available to SBI Funds Management Limited (the ‘Company’) and the Shareholders of the Company under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (‘the Act’) read with Income-tax Rules 2026, circulars, notifications issued thereto, as amended by the Finance Act 2026 (collectively, hereinafter referred to as ‘Indian Income-tax Regulations’) applicable for Tax Year 2026-2027:

# A. Special Tax Benefits available to the Company and its Group entities

# a. Lower corporate tax rate on income of domestic companies – Section 200 read with Section 205 of the Act

As per section 200 of the Act (erstwhile Section 115BAA of Income-tax Act, 1961), domestic companies are entitled to avail a concessional tax rate of 22% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), subject to the fulfillment of certain conditions specified in Section 200 read with Section 205 of the Act. The option to apply this tax rate is made available while filing return of income under Section 263 for such tax year (erstwhile to be exercised by filing of Form 10 -IC) and the option once exercised shall apply to subsequent tax years.

Further, for the purpose of opting the concessional tax rate of 22% under section 200 of the Act, the income is to be computed without taking into consideration the following deductions as provided in sub-section (1) of Section 200 of the Act read with Section 205:

1. Deduction under section 45(2) of the Act (Expenditure on scientific research);
2. Deduction under section 47(1)(b) of the Act (Expenditure on skill development);
3. Deduction under any provisions of Chapter VIII other than of section 146 or section 148 of the Act;
4. Deduction under section 33(8) of the Act (Additional depreciation);
5. Deduction under section 45(3)(a) or (b) or (c) of the Act (Expenditure on scientific research);
6. Deduction under section 46 of the Act (Deduction for capital expenditure of specified business);
7. Deduction under section 47(1)(a) of the Act (Deduction for agricultural extension project);
8. Deduction under section 48 of the Act (Deposit in tea development account, coffee development account and rubber development account);
9. Deduction under section 49 of the Act (Site restoration fund);
10. Deduction under section 144 of the Act (Deduction for units in Special Economic Zone);
11. No set-off of any loss carried forward or unabsorbed depreciation from any earlier tax year, if such loss or depreciation is attributable to any of the deductions referred from clause (1) to (10) above; and
12. No set-off of any loss or allowance for unabsorbed depreciation deemed so under section 116 of the Act, if such loss or depreciation is attributable to any of the deductions referred from clause (1) to (10) above.

Additionally, the provisions of section 206 of the Act i.e., Minimum Alternate Tax (‘MAT’) shall not apply to the Company once the option has been exercised under section 200 of the Act, as specified under sub-section (1) clause (q) of section 206 of the Act. Further, the Company will not be allowed to carry forward and set off any credit under section 206 of the Act, if any, commonly referred to as MAT credit.

The Company has opted for the lower corporate tax rate under section 115BAA of the erstwhile Income -tax Act, 1961 in Assessment Year 2020-2021 and has filed Form 10-IC with the Income-tax authorities on 25th January 2021, i.e., within the specified due date for filing Income-tax return.

# b. Deduction under Section 148 of the Act

Dividend income earned by the Company would be taxable in their hands at the 22% plus surcharge and cess.

Further, as per Section 148 of the Act, in case where the gross total income of a domestic company in any previous year includes any income by way of dividends from any other domestic company or a foreign company or a business trust, a deduction of an amount equal to so much of the amount of income by way of dividends received from such other domestic company or foreign company or business trust as does not exceed the amount of dividend distributed by it on or before the due date (i.e. the date one month prior to the date for furnishing the return of income under sub-section (1) of Section 263 of the Act) shall be allowed.

# c. Deductions in respect of employment of new employees – Section 146 of the Act

---


As per Section 146 of the Act, the Company to whom Section 63 of the Act applies and where total income includes profits and gains derived from business, is entitled to a deduction of an amount equal to thirty percent in respect of additional employee cost (relating to specified category of employees) incurred during the previous year. Such deduction is available for a period of three assessment years effective from the year in which such employment is provided. The eligibility to claim the deduction is subject to fulfilment of prescribed conditions specified in Section 146 of the Act. The Company is also required to submit the prescribed form with the Income-tax authorities within the specified due date.

# d. Deduction in respect of certain incomes of IFSC – Section 147 of the Act

Where the gross total income of a taxpayer, being a Unit of an IFSC, includes any income from any Unit of the IFSC from its business for which it has been approved for setting up in IFSC in a Special Economic Zone (SEZ), there shall be allowed, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of this section, a deduction from such income, of an amount equal to one hundred per cent of such income for any twenty consecutive tax years, at the option of the assessee, out of twenty-five years, beginning with the tax year in which the permission, or registration under the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50 of 2019) was obtained (‘IFSCA’). The taxpayer is also required to furnish a report in Form 35 along with the return of income for the purpose of claiming deduction under section 147 of the Act.

# B. Special Tax Benefits available to the Shareholders of the Company

# a. Dividend income

- Dividend income earned by the shareholders would be taxable in their hands at the applicable rates. Further, as per section 148 of the Act, in case where the gross total income of a domestic company in any previous year includes any income by way of dividends from any other domestic company or a foreign company or a business trust, a deduction of an amount equal to so much of the amount of income by way of dividends received from such other domestic company or foreign company or business trust as does not exceed the amount of dividend distributed by it on or before the due date (i.e. the date one month prior to the date for furnishing the return of income under sub-section (1) of section 263 of the Act) shall be allowed.
- In case of the shareholders who are individuals, Hindu Undivided Family, Association of Persons, Body of Individuals, whether incorporated or not and every artificial juridical person, the surcharge would be restricted to 15%, irrespective of the amount of dividend.
- Further, the shareholders would be entitled to take credit of the taxes withheld, if any, by the Company. Furthermore, as per section 207 of the Act, dividend income earned by a non-resident (not being a company) or by a foreign company, shall be taxed at the rate of 20% subject to fulfilment of prescribed conditions under the Act.

# b. Capital gains

# Characterization of gains from transfer of shares

- The characterization of the gains/losses, arising from sale/transfer of shares as business income or capital gains would depend on the nature of holding and various other factors. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has clarified in a circular that income arising from transfer of listed shares and securities, which are held for more than 12 months would be taxed as “Capital Gains” unless the shareholder itself treats these as its stock-in-trade and income arising from transfer thereof as its business income.

# Taxability on transfer of listed shares held as capital asset

- As per Section 198 of the Act, long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of equity shares are taxed at the rate of 12.5% (without indexation). Further, the surcharge on such long term capital gains is restricted to 15%.
- Section 198 of the Act stipulates that Securities Transaction Tax (STT) must be paid both at the time of acquisition and sale of equity shares, subject to the fulfilment of additional conditions prescribed under Notification No. 60/2018/F. No. 370142/9/2017-TPL dated 1 October 2018. It is important to note that tax under Section 198 will be levied only if the aggregate capital gains in a financial year exceed INR 1,25,000.
- As per Section 196 of the Act, short-term capital gains arising from transfer of equity shares on which STT is paid at the time of sale (also subject to the conditions of circular mentioned above), shall be taxed at the rate of 20%. Further, surcharge on such short-term capital gains under Section 196 of the Act is restricted to 15%.

# Deductions in computing capital gains

137



---


# In terms of Section 72 of the Act

In order to arrive at the quantum of capital gains, the following amounts would be deductible from the full value of the consideration:

- a) Cost of acquisition of shares; and
- b) Expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of shares

# Other provisions

# Treaty benefits

As per Section 159(4) of the Act, non-resident shareholders will be entitled to be governed by the beneficial provisions under the respective Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), if any, applicable to such non-residents. This is subject to fulfilment of conditions prescribed to avail treaty benefits.

# Set-off and carry forward of losses

As per Section 111 of the Act, short-term capital losses incurred during the year are allowed to be set-off against short-term or long-term capital gains of the said year. Balance losses, if any may be carried forward for eight tax years for claiming set-off against subsequent years’ short-term or long-term capital gains. Long-term capital losses incurred during the year are allowed to be set-off only against long term capital gains. Balance loss, if any, could be carried forward for eight years for claiming set-off against subsequent year’s long-term capital gains.

# Notes:

1. These special tax benefits are dependent on the Company or its shareholders fulfilling the conditions prescribed under the relevant provisions of the Indian Income-tax Regulations. Hence, the ability of the Company or its shareholders to derive the tax benefits is dependent upon fulfilling such conditions, which based on the business imperatives, the Company or its shareholders may or may not choose to fulfil.
2. The special tax benefits discussed in the Statement are not exhaustive and are only intended to provide general information to the investors and hence, it is neither designed nor intended to be a substitute for professional tax advice, which the investors may wish to take before making any investments. In view of the individual nature of the tax consequences accompanied by the changing tax laws, each investor is advised to consult his or her own tax consultant with respect to the specific tax implications arising out of their participation in the issue.
3. The Statement is prepared based on information available with the management of the Company and there is no assurance that:
1. the Company or its shareholders will continue to obtain these benefits in future;
2. the conditions prescribed for availing the benefits have been/ would be met with; and
3. the revenue authorities/courts will concur with the view expressed herein.
4. The above views are based on the existing provisions of law and our interpretation of the law, which are subject to change from time to time. The new Income-tax Act, 2025 is effective from 1st April 2026. We do not assume responsibility to update the views consequent to any changes. # MACROECONOMIC SCENARIO IN INDIA

# Global macroeconomic outlook

The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World Economic Outlook, April 2026, states that the global economy showed remarkable resilience in calendar year 2025, with global real gross domestic product (GDP) growth reaching 3.4%. Despite initial uncertainties pertaining to tariffs imposed by the United States (US) and its potential impact on global growth, trade disruptions remained limited, given the frontloading of imports in the first half of the year and swift reorganisation of supply chains to redirect trade flows.

The global geopolitical landscape is going through a radical change, marked by the ongoing conflict in West Asia and a shift in traditional power dynamics. The IMF projects the world GDP growth to moderate to 3.1% in 2026 and recover to 3.2% in 2027. The prolonged conflict has started impacting commodity prices, inflation and financial conditions adversely, potentially testing global and country-specific economic resilience. These challenges are particularly pronounced in countries that are not directly involved in the conflict but rely on West Asia for various needs.

Global inflation is expected to increase to 4.4% in calendar year 2026, reflecting expected higher energy and food prices, before falling to 3.7% in 2027. Inflation in China is projected to rise from low levels, while India’s is expected to return to near-target levels after a significant drop in 2025, driven by subdued food prices.

Meanwhile, the India-Europe free trade agreement (FTA) finalised on January 27, 2026, aims to reshape trade, with the European Union dropping tariffs on 99.5% of Indian exports over seven years, and India reducing tariffs on European luxury cars (from 110% to 10% over five years) and wines (from 150% to 75%). The deal serves as a strategic hedge to reduce dependency on China and the US.

On the other hand, the FTA signed with New Zealand in April 2026, aims to enhance exports, support MSMEs, attract investment, facilitate skills mobility and promote broader economic cooperation. It grants immediate zero-duty access for 100% of Indian exports to New Zealand, subject to product-specific rules of origin, benefitting key sectors such as textiles, engineering, pharmaceuticals, marine products and chemicals. This FTA further serves as a gateway to the wider Oceania and Pacific Island markets.

On the domestic turf, India’s National Statistics Office (NSO) estimated real GDP growth at 7.4% in fiscal 2026, driven by strong demand, high infrastructure spending and improvements in manufacturing and services. India has mitigated external shocks such as US tariffs on account of diversified trade partnerships. However, the conflict in West Asia has reduced India’s forex reserves to $681 billion as of May 22, 2026.

---

# India to be the fastest-growing major economy

India's growth is significantly outperforming other major economies and emerging markets, fuelled by strong domestic demand, robust consumption and improved financial conditions. High consumer spending is enabling India to outpace China's growth, which is projected to be ~4.4% in calendar year 2026 and ~4.0% in 2027.

We project inflation based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to rise to 5.1% on average in fiscal 2027 from an estimated 2.0% in the previous fiscal as food inflation is expected to normalise from the lows of the past year. This is based on the expectation that crude oil prices will average $90-95 per barrel in fiscal 2027 compared with an estimated ~$70 per barrel last fiscal. The forecast is in line with recent trends as CPI inflation rose to 3.4% in March 2026 from 3.2% in February 2026 but remained within the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) target range of 2-6%. Given the uptick in inflation, we expect the RBI to maintain the current policy rates by keeping a close watch on the evolving inflation trajectory.

India's nominal GDP has been growing at a rapid pace, with an average annual growth rate of ~10% over the past decade. As per the IMF, India’s nominal GDP is estimated to have risen 8.94% in calendar year 2025 and is projected to grow further by ~11% in calendar year 2026. This is one of the fastest growth rates among major economies, followed by Brazil with a growth rate of ~6% in calendar year 2026. Cross-country comparison also show that India’s growth has generally been higher than in most large developed markets and broadly comparable to leading emerging economies, supporting corporate earnings growth, credit demand, and the creation of investable assets. For managed funds, this is important because the overall size and durability of the opportunity set typically tracks nominal GDP expansion and the formalisation of economic activity. In addition, strong GDP growth tends to lift household incomes and savings, which then strengthens investment demand. Faster growth also helps capital markets expand, supporting mark-to-market gains and accelerating asset accumulation.

India also benefits from a large, young population, with a significant share below age 35, which can provide a demographic dividend and support sustained economic growth. At the same time, India’s digital economy is expanding quickly, with a large and growing internet user base, rising mobile penetration, and increasing adoption of digital payments. This is creating new avenues for growth and job creation.

# RBI held the repo rate unchanged at 5.25% in June 2026

The RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) initiated a monetary policy easing cycle in 2025 through calibrated repo rate cuts to support economic growth. A 25-basis points (bps) cut in February lowered the repo rate to 6.25%, followed by another 25-bps reduction in April, alongside a shift in policy stance to 'accommodative' from 'neutral'. In June, the central bank intensified its easing efforts, with a 50-bps rate cut and shifting its policy stance to ‘neutral’.

The MPC kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25% at its June 2026 meeting and maintained a 'neutral' stance, signalling continued confidence that India’s economic growth will remain resilient, driven by a significant increase in capital expenditure outlined in the Union Budget 2026. The budget increased the capital expenditure outlay for fiscal 2027 to Rs 12.2 lakh crore, which accounts for 4.4% of the GDP. The MPC also cited sustained growth in private consumption and fixed capital formation as factors supporting its optimistic outlook. That said, it warned that external risks persist, including the expected El Niño and the ongoing conflict in West Asia. Higher energy and other input costs arising from the conflict, along with disrupted supply chains, could weigh on overall economic activity.

At its June 2026 meeting, the RBI also announced a series of measures aimed at attracting foreign capital. These included the removal of taxes on income and gains earned by foreign investors from Indian government securities, a step intended to make India’s sovereign debt market more appealing to global investors. The long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax on government securities has been reduced from 12.5% to nil, while the withholding tax on interest income from these securities has also been scrapped, bringing the rate down from 20% to nil. As a result, returns earned by foreign investors from investments in Indian sovereign bonds will effectively become tax-free.

The stable repo rate is expected to support the economy by allowing banks to maintain current lending rates, thereby encouraging borrowing and spending. A stable, accommodative-to-neutral monetary policy stance typically boosts investor confidence. This, along with lower borrowing costs and steady liquidity make investors more comfortable in taking risk, including investing in equities. For retail investors, lower uncertainty can support continued investments in systematic investment plans (SIPs) and higher long-term allocations to mutual funds, which can translate into stronger assets under management (AUM) growth for asset management companies (AMCs).

Overall, this policy environment is favourable for mutual fund houses, as debt funds can benefit from lower yields and a steadier rate outlook, equity funds from improved growth expectations and stronger valuations, and hybrid funds from higher demand for balanced exposure. For AMCs, it can mean higher AUM, better fee potential, stronger product demand and improved sentiment. The main opportunity is to align debt, equity and hybrid offerings with themes of lower rates, resilient growth and India’s capex-driven investment cycle.

While the ongoing conflict in West Asia remains a risk to key supply chains and external demand, the RBI expects structural reforms, including rationalisation of the goods and services tax (GST) to partly offset these headwinds. Also, the standing deposit facility rate remains at 5.00%, while the marginal standing facility rate and the bank rate have been reduced to 5.50%, further supporting the stability of the financial system.

# CPI inflation to average at 5.1% in fiscal 2027 owing to the West Asia conflict

Inflation based on the revised CPI series, with 2024 as the base year, rose to 3.48% in April 2026 from 3.40% in March 2026 as food inflation normalised further, driven by an uptick in food (4.2% in April vs 3.9% in March). It eased however, for fuel (0.7% in April vs 1.7% in March) inflation.

Within the non-food category, fuel and transport inflation are already facing pressures from higher oil and gas prices and supply shocks arising from the conflict in West Asia.

We project CPI inflation to average 5.1% in fiscal 2027. While food prices are expected to remain stable, potential El Niño conditions may introduce uncertainties. Food inflation is likely to normalise from its fiscal 2026 lows, with weather-related disruptions posing an upside risk.

# Key growth drivers

# 2. India has the world’s largest population

As per the 2011 Census, India's population was approximately 1.3 billion, comprising nearly 187 million households. We estimate the population logged a CAGR of 1.1% between fiscals 2011 and 2021, reaching 1.4 billion. The population is projected to cross 1.5 billion by fiscal 2030, with the number of households expected to increase to around 385 million, representing a CAGR of 4.6% between fiscals 2021 and 2031. This indicates a significant expansion in the country's demographic landscape. India has the largest young population (15-29 years) among the major economies, with over 380 million individuals in this age group.

# 3. Favourable demographics

India has the largest youth population in the world, with a median age of 28 years. Also, ~90% of the country’s population is below 60 years. In 2025, at 26%, India was estimated to have the highest share of young working population (15 -29 years) among the major developed and developing economies. We expect India’s large working-age population, along with rapid



---


urbanisation and rising affluence, to drive economic growth. This demographic tailwind is also expected to support higher SIP participation and long-term flows into mutual funds, benefiting mutual fund AMCs through stronger AUM growth.

# 4. Rising urbanisation

Urbanisation is a key driver of India’s economic growth, as it is expected to spur substantial investments in infrastructure development, creating jobs, fostering modern consumer services and increasing mobilisation of savings. India’s urban population has consistently risen, from 23% of the total population in fiscal 1981 to 28% in fiscal 2001 and further to about 36% in fiscal 2026. By fiscal 2031, 41% of India’s population is projected to live in urban areas, although still lower than in developed nations.

# 5. Increasing per capita GDP

India’s per capita net national income at constant prices grew 5.5% in fiscal 2026, reflecting robust economic growth and the government’s continued endeavour to make the country an upper middle-income economy. As per IMF estimates, the country’s per capita income (at constant prices) is expected to clock a CAGR of 5-6% in real terms between fiscals 2025 and 2028, indicating a gradual increase in average income levels. This will help a larger portion of the population, particularly the emerging middle class, meet and exceed the income threshold needed for necessities such as food, housing and essential basic services. As affordability increases, households are likely to shift their spending and saving patterns, moving from basic savings toward insurance and retirement solutions, and then into market-linked products such as mutual funds. Over time, they may further diversify into additional investment categories including private markets, real assets, and structured yield products. Collectively, this can deepen the financial sector, enhance long-term stability through sustained investment, and channel more capital into the broader economy.

Expanding middle-India population to help sustain economic growth

The proportion of middle India (defined as households with annual income of Rs 0.2-1.0 million) has been on the rise over the past decade and is expected to continue increasing with the rising GDP and household incomes. As per our estimate, middle-income households are expected to increase to 181 million by fiscal 2030 from an estimated 41 million in fiscal 2012. A large number of households that have entered this bracket in the past few years are likely from semi-urban and rural areas. As per the 76ᵗʰ round (2018) of the National Sample Survey, 83.3% of households were living in pucca dwelling units, compared with 74.6% in the 69ᵗʰ round (2012).

# 6. India’s gross domestic savings rate was higher than the global average in calendar year 2024

In calendar year 2024, India’s gross domestic savings were about 30% of GDP, up from roughly 13% in 1975 and slightly above the global average of around 26%. A structurally strong savings rate reflects household balance-sheet stability and the capacity for capital formation in the economy.

Higher domestic savings help support long-term investment, infrastructure development, and credit expansion by channelling households’ accumulated savings into the economy through various financial assets and investments over time. As middle-class incomes and savings grow, this becomes a key driver of economic growth through increased domestic savings and investment.

Unlike most other countries where financial savings dominate, physical assets constitute the majority of household savings in India. In fiscal 2014, household savings in physical form in the country stood at 62%. This decreased to 47% in fiscal 2021 as pandemic-induced nationwide lockdowns slowed down construction of houses. With the lifting of lockdowns post the pandemic, the share surged to 63% in fiscal 2022 and 70% in fiscal 2024, owing to an increase in construction of houses. We expect the share of financial assets in net household savings to increase over the next five years, as elevated inflation after the pandemic could have further goaded investors to move to higher-yielding instruments in real terms. Interestingly, households are also opting to hold more cash after enduring the pandemic shock.

Mutual fund investments by households have grown rapidly in the recent past, from mere 3% of their annual savings in 2020 to around 13% in 2025 reflecting the deepening financialisation of domestic savings. Investments through systematic investment plans (SIPs), mostly opted by individuals, continued to rise in fiscal 2026. Households are increasingly shifting away from deposit-based savings towards equities, mutual funds and small savings schemes, reflecting a growing appetite for risk and rising financialisation. This growing share of financial assets in net household savings presents an opportunity for AMCs, since households are seeking reliable and credible channels to invest their savings for better returns over time.

# Rising number of wealthy individuals to drive investments across asset classes

India’s robust economic and entrepreneurial ecosystem is poised to drive a significant increase in the number of high-net-worth individuals (HNIs), ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNIs) and family offices. These affluent individuals have substantially transformed India's financial wealth accumulation landscape by diversifying their investments from traditional financial instruments to higher-yielding assets, such as mutual funds and equities.

Despite this shift, a substantial portion of household savings still consist of bank and non-bank deposits, which grew to Rs 12.5 trillion in fiscal 2025 from Rs 8.4 trillion in fiscal 2022. Mutual funds have emerged as the fastest-growing segment of financial savings, rising to Rs 4.7 trillion in fiscal 2025 from Rs 1.6 trillion in fiscal 2022, clocking a remarkable CAGR of 42.6%.

Mutual fund AUM as a percentage of bank deposits has increased steadily, reflecting strong growth in mutual fund penetration relative to traditional bank savings. After a brief moderation in fiscal 2023, the ratio accelerated from fiscal 2024 onwards, indicating rising investor preference for market-linked investment avenues.

SBI Mutual Fund market leadership is further supported by favourable industry tailwinds, including growing mutual fund penetration in household savings, favourable demographics with a young and increasingly financially literate population, rising income levels and savings rates, and increasing investor awareness driven by industry-wide investor education initiatives.

# 7. Financial penetration to rise with increasing awareness of financial products

As per the Periodic Labour Force Survey Annual Report 2023-24, India’s overall literacy rate for individuals aged 7 and above is 80.9%, which is below the world literacy rate of ~88%, as reported by the World Bank. However, according to the National Financial Literacy and Inclusion Survey 2019, only 27% of Indian population is financially literate, highlighting substantial untapped potential for the financial services industry. The survey defines financial literacy as a combination of awareness, knowledge, skills, attitude and behaviour necessary to make sound financial decisions and ultimately achieve individual financial well-being.

The government and financial institutions have launched several financial literacy programmes (such as the National Centre for Financial Education and Swabhimaan) to educate people about the benefits of financial planning and management. These programmes aim to improve financial literacy among the marginalised sections of the society and empower them to make informed financial decisions.

With the rise in financial literacy, demand for financial products, especially in smaller cities, has seen a major uptick in recent years. We expect financial penetration to increase going forward on account of the increase in financial literacy.

# 8. Accelerating financial inclusion in India

As per the Global Findex Database 2024, ~53% of the world’s 650 million unbanked adults live in only eight countries—India, Bangladesh, China, Indonesia, Egypt, Mexico, Nigeria and Pakistan. Despite high account ownership rates, India’s massive population means it remains among the countries with a high number of unbanked adults. The 2025 report (reporting on 2024 data) indicates that, while 89% of Indian adults now own a financial account, in 2024, 14% of adults (representing a significant portion of the global unbanked population) in India still had inactive accounts, which presents immense opportunity for financial institutions to increase financial inclusion within the country.

# 9. Trend in demat accounts in India

In recent years, the participation of individuals in the equity market has increased, driven by higher financial literacy, a growing middle class, digitalisation and enhanced accessibility. India has witnessed a surge in financial literacy, driven by the rise of do-it-yourself investment platforms and discount brokers. These platforms have simplified access to stocks, mutual funds and other financial products, making investing easier and more affordable. With zero or low brokerage fees, real-time market insights and user-friendly apps, retail investors find it easier to access these products. Government initiatives, digital banking and fintech innovations further boost financial inclusion. The number of demat accounts in India expanded at a 24.4% CAGR.



---


over fiscals 2016-2026. By March 2026, the total exceeded 224.5 million. This data highlights the increasing awareness and willingness of people to participate in capital markets for trading.

# 10. Convenience, affordability and diversification are attracting new retail investors

Mutual funds invest in a broad portfolio of stocks, bonds and other securities by pooling the capital of several investors. By spreading risk, diversification reduces the impact of underperformance of an individual investment on the overall portfolio of the investor, providing a balanced and more stable portfolio. Experienced fund managers oversee mutual funds, access markets, choose investments and modify portfolios in response to shifting market conditions. Retail investors lacking the time or competence to actively manage their investments are drawn to this expertise. This investment avenue allows them to start investing with a relatively small amount of money, and the affordability allows a larger number of investors to start their investment journey, including those who may not have significant capital to invest in individual stocks or bonds. Investors can choose from a range of tailored schemes that match their risk tolerance and financial objectives. SIPs offer investors the flexibility to invest variable amounts at a time and frequency that suits their needs while building discipline. This investment route allows investors to take advantage of market volatility over time and gain compounding benefits. As these funds are regulated by financial institutions, it increases the confidence of retail investors.

# 11. Active participation in the stock market by retail investors to seek higher returns

The government’s efforts to promote financial literacy have encouraged retail investors to get involved by putting funds directly in equities. Retail investment in India has surged with an increasing number of demat accounts, driven by digital accessibility, low-cost trading and financial education. This growth is largely fuelled by Gen Z and women, who are increasingly seeking better returns and are influenced by social media and financial awareness.

Direct equity has the potential to offer higher returns than other investment options. Investing in individual stocks also provides retail investors with educational experience. It allows them to learn about financial markets and economic trends, thus promoting financial literacy. This is unlike mutual funds, where investors pay fees for professional management. Investing in direct equity allows individuals to avoid these fees, potentially leading to lower overall investment cost. Investing in direct equity gives investors more control over their portfolios and they can make decisions based on their own research preference and risk tolerance rather than relying on fund managers.

However, retail investors engaging in direct investing in equity face risks, including the absence of professional guidance, susceptibility to market volatility, limited diversification opportunities, potential emotional decision-making and a higher risk of financial loss.

# 12. Better access and control over investment are driving small cases among retail investors

Small cases are curated stock portfolios centred around specific themes or investment strategies; retail investors may appreciate the focus on sectoral or investment themes that align with their preference or beliefs. Small cases provide investors better access and control over securities since the shares are credited directly in their demat accounts, allowing them to exit any investment since there is no exit load.

The potential risk and return in small cases are relatively high as compared with mutual funds. They are usually more volatile, with the risk concentrated in a specific strategy or theme.

# 13. Digitalisation aided by technology to play pivotal role in economic growth

Technology is expected to play an important role by progressively reducing the cost of reaching out to smaller markets. India has seen a tremendous rise in fintech adoption in the past few years.

Among many government initiatives, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is playing a pivotal role towards financial inclusion. It provides a single-click digital interface across systems for smartphones linked to bank accounts and facilitates easy transactions using a simple authentication method. The increased adoption of UPI has sent the volume of digital transactions surging in the past few years, as seen in the section below.

Apart from the financial services industry, digitalisation in other industries such as retail will also play an important role in economic growth.

# 14. Increased UPI transactions are fuelling India’s digital economy

Usage of UPI as a preferred payment method has jumped from 22.3 billion in fiscal 2021 to 241.6 billion in fiscal 2026 in terms of volume and from Rs 41 trillion to Rs 314.2 trillion in terms of value. This trend underscores the technological innovations driving financial inclusion and accelerating digital economy.

# 15. Rising income-tax returns indicate progression towards a formal economy

The number of income-tax returns (ITR) filed by individuals has risen from 60 million in fiscal 2019 to 76 million in fiscal 2024. This uptrend reflects increasing tax compliance, a growing workforce, improving financial transparency and economic stability, underscoring India’s progress towards formal economy. The rise in ITR filings indicates more individuals are entering the formal financial system, which can lead to better access to credit, insurance and other financial services.

# Key announcement and changes in the capital markets

# 16. Bond markets

Both gross and net borrowings from dated securities are higher than expected at Rs 17.2 lakh crore and Rs 11.7 lakh crore, respectively. However, a significant portion has been allocated for refinancing past liabilities rather than new spending. The Centre has set net market borrowing at Rs 11.7 lakh crore for this fiscal, about Rs 50,000 crore higher than in the preceding one, indicating a measured increase to support greater capital expenditure. Gross market borrowing is projected at Rs 17.2 lakh crore, a substantial rise from the current year, mainly due to the maturity profile of government securities, with redemptions in this fiscal estimated at Rs 5.47 lakh crore. This could push up sovereign yields in the near term.

The announcement of Rs 2 trillion support under the Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) will benefit states that meet the requirements for stronger fiscal positions and higher project readiness. The impact is likely to be frontloaded since SASCI disbursements are typically released earlier, subject to project approval. Eligible states may, therefore, defer or reduce state development loan issuances in the first half of the year, which may lead to lower spreads than at present.

The announcement of the market-making framework aims to structurally deepen liquidity and improve price discovery in the corporate bond market. A stronger secondary market could help widen market participation in corporate bonds. Derivatives on corporate bond indices will also help enhance market depth.

The introduction of total return swaps on corporate bonds would enable synthetic exposure to bond returns without necessitating ownership of the underlying instruments. This is expected to enhance risk-hedging efficiency, facilitate broader investor participation and support the development of a more resilient and liquid corporate bond market. The product could improve leverage and unlock value through hedging strategies for AIFs and SIFs (specialised investment funds).

The additional incentive of Rs 1 billion to be provided over and above the current Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation scheme, for a single municipal bond issuance of more than Rs 10 billion, could encourage municipal bond.



---


# 17. Equity markets

The increase of STT on futures to 0.05% from 0.02% at present and on options premium and exercise of options from 0.1% and 0.125% to 0.15%, respectively, will lead to moderation in excessive future and options activity. It will also lead to deeper investor interest in long-term investment products.

The change in taxation of buyback from deemed dividend to capital gains at slab rates for shareholders is positive since it reduces investor tax liability.

# 18. Alternative assets - AIFs, REITs and InvITs

The specialised SME Growth Fund with a dedicated corpus of Rs 100 billion will increase the availability of long-term institutional funding to MSMEs. It also expands the set of investible opportunities available to AIFs.

The infusion of an additional Rs 20 billion into the Self-Reliant India Fund, established in 2021, will sustain support for micro enterprises and ensure continued access to risk capital.

The Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund, an infrastructure investment fund (InvIT), is aimed at providing partial credit guarantees to lenders. This will strengthen confidence among lenders and investors. It could help build a deeper corporate bond market, while enhancing the investible universe for real estate and infrastructure trusts.

The proposal to accelerate the recycling of significant real estate assets of CPSEs by setting up dedicated real estate and infrastructure trusts (REITs) will significantly expand the supply of income-generating assets and improve funding efficiency. This could help build a larger market for REITs.

# 19. Foreign investments

The RBI, in June 2026, proposed expanding the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) for government securities by bringing all new issuances of 15-year, 30-year, and 40-year government securities under the category, while removing short-term investment limits and concentration norms for foreign portfolio investors in government bonds. It also proposed doubling the individual investment limit for NRIs and OCIs in listed Indian companies to 10% from 5% and raising the aggregate limit to 24% from 10%. This facility will also be extended to all individual Persons Resident Outside India (PROIs), broadening participation in Indian equity markets and aligning overseas investment rules with recent Budget announcements.

The RBI also introduced a concessional forex swap facility for external commercial borrowings by public sector undertakings and extended support for FCNR(B) deposits.

The comprehensive review of FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules could help enhance foreign flows into equity instruments, units of AIFs, REITs and InvITs, mutual funds, equity exchange-traded funds and equity tranches of securitisation structures, among others.

The increase in investment limit for individual persons resident outside India (PROI), under the Portfolio Investment Scheme, will enhance flows to Indian equities and help further diversify the investor base. The investment limit under the scheme is proposed to be increased from 5% to 10%, pushing up the overall investment limit to 24%, from the current 10%.

# 20. Sovereign gold bonds

The government is to provide exemption from capital gains tax for investment in sovereign gold bonds only where such bonds are subscribed at the time of original issue and held continuously until redemption on maturity. This initiative aims to bring uniformity and clarity to the tax treatment of sovereign gold bonds. It aligns the exemption with the original intent of encouraging long-term participation in the scheme.

OVERVIEW OF CAPITAL MARKETS IN INDIA

# 21. Domestic investors cushioned capital markets amid global uncertainty last fiscal

In fiscal 2026, India’s equity markets remained under pressure amid geopolitical, trade and tariff-related uncertainties and higher crude oil prices. Strong foreign portfolio outflows further weighed on sentiment as investors shifted toward cheaper and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven global markets. The economy showed resilience, aided by lower inflation, accommodative financial conditions and technology-led investment. However, the equilibrium weakened towards the end of the fiscal following the West Asia conflict, which added a new inflationary impact in the form of rising energy costs and supply chain disruptions. Amid all this, domestic investor flows kept the capital market stable. According to the National Stock Exchange (NSE), the fiscal saw net inflows of Rs 8.5 trillion from domestic institutional investors (DIIs), riding on steady systematic investment plan (SIP) contributions, which averaged Rs 29,132 crore a month. As on March 31, 2026, India’s market capitalisation stood at Rs 412 trillion, translating into an annualised growth of 24% over fiscals 2020-2026.

# 22. India’s market capitalisation as a proportion of GDP vs major economies

India’s stock market capitalisation-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio increased to 133.5% in 2025 from 95.4% in 2020. In fiscal 2026, the market capitalisation of NSE-listed companies closed flat at 0.1% at ~Rs 411.3 trillion vs ~Rs 410.9 trillion in fiscal 2025 on account of trade policy and economic uncertainty.

The Nifty 50 recorded a strong rally in fiscal 2024, supported by robust inflows from DIIs and FIIs. The upward momentum continued into the following fiscal, driven by sustained DII buying even as FIIs turned net sellers.

In fiscal 2026, FII selling intensified amid persistent global trade-related uncertainty, which weighed on investor sentiment. A sharp depreciation in the Indian rupee further accelerated capital outflows, as foreign investors showed an inclination to relatively better-valued and AI-led global markets. The prolonged conflict in West Asia, along with emerging risks to India’s inflation, trade balance and fiscal position, added to the pressure. As a result, FIIs recorded a net outflow of Rs 1.8 trillion in fiscal 2026, the highest on record.

Despite global headwinds, DIIs continued to provide a strong counterbalance to FII selling, underscoring the depth and resilience of India’s domestic investor base. In fiscal 2026, DIIs net-invested a record Rs 8.5 trillion, marking a 39.8% increase on-year. This was supported by strong retail participation through mutual funds, particularly via SIPs. SIP inflows reached a record Rs 32,087 crore in March 2026, with average monthly inflows rising to Rs 29,132 crore in fiscal 2026 from Rs 24,113 crore in fiscal 2025.

Indian mutual funds also maintained elevated cash reserves amid improved market liquidity, enabling fund managers to deploy capital swiftly when attractive opportunities emerge. Overall, the continued strength of DII inflows highlights the growing maturity, risk appetite and participation of domestic investors, reinforcing the resilience of Indian equity markets despite sustained FII outflows and global uncertainty.

# 26. Key growth drivers

Improving per capita net national income, higher gross domestic savings as a share of GDP and rising digital payments are strengthening India’s capital market outlook. As incomes increase, individuals are more likely to explore a range of financial investment options, which can deepen participation in capital markets. Other key growth drivers include:

# 27. Demographics supporting folio growth in capital markets

India’s demographics are a major tailwind for capital markets. In 2025, India had the largest youth population globally, with a median age of 28 years and roughly 90% of the population under 60. India was also estimated to have the highest share of young working-age population (15 to 29 years) among major developed and developing economies at 26%. We expect this category to underpin economic growth, supported by rapid urbanisation and rising affluence.

For long-term investment products, rising life expectancy and growing retirement and wealth-building aspirations among the working-age population are also increasing demand for equity and mutual fund investments in capital markets.

# 28. Regulations and initiatives by SEBI and exchanges to aid penetration and growth in capital markets

Faster settlement cycles and the transition to electronic trading have improved overall market efficiency. In addition, SEBI has introduced reforms aimed at increasing transparency, strengthening investor protection and enhancing market functioning. Broader reforms such as the goods and services tax, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 have also helped create a more structured market environment. In addition, they are aimed at making the capital market safer and more secure for investors. A few are listed below:

Application Supported by Blocked Amount (ASBA) is a mechanism applied to initial public offerings (IPOs) or follow-on public offerings. ASBA creates a direct channel for funds flow between the clearing corporation and investors and reduces fraud in the handling of investor money by brokers. UPI ASBA lets retail investors apply for IPOs up to Rs 5 lakh using their



---


broker's platform or app. Funds remain in the investor’s bank account, earning interest until shares are allotted. The application money is simply blocked, rather than being immediately debited. Block mechanism facility involves the blocking of shares in the investor’s demat account whenever they want to make a sale. Shorter settlement cycle from T+2 to T+1. Markets were functioning on a T+2 settlement cycle for a prolonged period. In January 2023, SEBI brought in the T+1 settlement cycle to settle trades within a day or 24 hours. The move was made in view of operational efficiency, faster fund remittances, quicker share delivery and the ease of market participants.

Other important regulatory and structural changes include permitting mutual funds to invest in real estate investment trusts and infrastructure investment trusts, allowing e-wallets for mutual fund purchases and enabling stock exchange infrastructure to support mutual fund purchase and redemption (such as BSE STAR MF and NSE NMF). Listing requirements have been eased for startups and small and medium enterprises, while onboarding has been streamlined through Aadhaar-based KYC. IPO transparency has improved through additional disclosures, including key performance indicators. The introduction of MF Central as a single-window investment management platform has further strengthened the ecosystem.

Overall, these measures have supported growth in India’s capital markets by making transactions easier, more convenient, more reliable and faster.

# 29. Increasing smartphone penetration will drive growth in mobile stock trading

By fiscal-end 2026, India had ~1,162 million wireless subscribers. With mobile networks, internet connectivity and electricity expanding into remote areas, smartphone and internet access is increasing. This should further support growth in mobile trading among retail investors. It is likely to particularly benefit brokers and asset management companies that keep investing in technology and trading platforms, enabling them to offer a better trading and investing experience than their competitors.

# 30. SGX Nifty shifts to GIFT City; GIFT City on the path to becoming a global hub

The SGX Nifty was shifted to GIFT City, Gandhinagar in mid-2023. NSE IFSC – SGX Connect was launched in July 2022, which marked the beginning of a transition of liquidity riding on SGX Nifty to NSE IFSC. It was known as the GIFT NIFTY Index, widening the liquidity pool for Nifty products there. This means, that derivative contracts worth ~$750 crore, earlier traded from Singapore, shifted to India.

GIFT Nifty includes GIFT Nifty 50, GIFT Nifty Bank, GIFT Nifty Financial Services and GIFT Nifty IT derivative contracts. Many initiatives are underway with respect to GIFT International Exchange that will help Indian markets extend their reach among global investors through direct engagement. It is expected Indian entities will soon be allowed to directly list on NSE IFSC, which would help Indian companies access capital from global investors. This brings GIFT City a step closer to becoming a global competitor to other financial hubs such as Dubai, Mauritius, Singapore, etc.

# 31. Demand for wealth advisors is surging with increasing customer wealth

As customer wealth and per capita income rise, the demand for wealth advisors is surging. This trend emphasises the growing complexity of financial portfolios and the increasing need for personalised wealth management services. With higher net worth comes a greater array of investment opportunities, tax considerations, and estate planning intricacies, necessitating expert guidance to navigate effectively.

Wealth advisors play a pivotal role in assisting clients optimise financial resources, mitigate risks and achieve long-term objectives by delivering tailored solutions.

# 32. Rising demand for corporate debt issuance

Over the years, capital markets have played a pivotal role in the development of the Indian economy. As the country surges ahead, the Indian capital market is expected to play a greater role. The corporate bond market is a crucial element of the Indian capital market. Persistent efforts by the government and SEBI in the past few years have enabled a nascent corporate bond market to move in the direction of maturity.

Many companies have issued equity through IPOs over the past couple of years, raising capital to finance their growth. With the economy growing and businesses gaining scale, more companies are expected to explore raising equity from capital markets. On the demand side, retail participation, index-linked funds and mechanisms to improve liquidity will be enablers. Attracting foreign capital is also crucial to bridge the emerging supply-demand gap, especially given the crowding-out by gilts stemming from the government’s huge borrowing programme.

We believe the following measures will enable the Indian debt capital market to play an important role:

---



• Implementing the draft Reserve Bank of India (Credit Derivatives) Directions, 2021, to facilitate the development of the credit default swaps (CDS) market. This will allow banks, non-banking finance companies, insurers, pension funds, mutual funds, alternate investment funds and foreign portfolio investors to write CDS.

• Enhancing retail participation via tax sops to investments in debt mutual funds (similar to equity-linked savings schemes) and ensure parity in capital gains tax between equity and debt products.

• Improving liquidity in the market by fast-tracking the setting up of an institution to provide secondary market liquidity to corporate bonds, develop the Limited Purpose Clearance Corporation for corporate bond repos and allow corporate bonds as collateral under the RBI’s India’s liquidity adjustment facility window.

• Attracting domestic and foreign capital through exchange-traded funds and other index-linked bond funds, which offer lower costs, more transparency, better liquidity and potential to build diversified portfolios.

• Profiling the ESG (environmental, social and governance) status of Indian corporates to attract foreign capital into the Indian debt capital markets.

# 33. Increasing participation of domestic players in investments

The number of unique client codes surpassed 250 million in fiscal 2026, indicating the continued structural expansion of India’s retail investor base. Supported by strong participation in domestic capital markets, DIIs sustained record inflows into Indian equities, backed by solid macroeconomic fundamentals and the significant returns generated by the Indian market in recent years. Over the past five years, DIIs have remained consistent net buyers of Indian equities, delivering total net buying of more than Rs 21.4 trillion. They have continued to support the markets even as FIIs have turned net sellers since fiscal 2022 (except in fiscal 2024).

# Encouraging outlook on Indian capital markets

The Indian stock market recorded a strong performance in fiscal 2026 despite facing several headwinds such as tariff-related trade uncertainty, fluctuations in crude oil prices, weakness in the rupee and rising inflationary pressure due to the prolonged West-Asia conflict.

We have a constructive outlook on the capital markets, largely driven by:

- Initiatives taken by financial regulators towards financial education that would empower investors in making informed decisions and encourage participation in the market.
- The shift to the new tax regime introduced in Union Budget 2025, and its continuation in Budget 2026. This is expected to increase the disposable income of investors, creating greater investable surplus and enabling higher levels of investment. The revised income-tax exemption threshold of Rs 12 lakh will boost disposable income, encouraging higher savings and investments in capital markets, driving retail participation and enhancing liquidity in equities and mutual funds.
- Reduction of fiscal deficit and market borrowing, which were in line with market expectations thereby having limited impact on government yields. With reduction in interest rates, the bond market would be conducive to higher bond prices since existing bonds with higher yields become more attractive.
- The government is encouraging cities to float municipal bonds in a bid to grow the bond market. Further, financial market measures towards market-linked debentures and listed debentures will bridge tax arbitrage and would attract investor flows in the future.

Historically, India’s securities market, like those of other developing markets, has shown significant volatility across both broad indices and individual securities. Over the past decade, Indian equities have experienced alternating periods of upward and downward price trends. In 2020, global capital markets, including Indian equities, faced sharp volatility due to the pandemic and related responses. Since then, Indian markets have generally followed a positive trend, with occasional bouts of volatility. During these periods, DIIs have played a crucial role in cushioning market moves, highlighting the growing maturity of India’s investor base.

# MUTUAL FUNDS INDUSTRY IN INDIA

The Indian mutual fund industry has evolved from a government-sponsored savings vehicle in the 1960s into one of the world's fastest-growing asset management markets. The industry began with the establishment of Unit Trust of India (UTI) in 1963. UTI launched the iconic Unit Scheme 1964 (US-64), which became the primary investment avenue for retail savers seeking exposure to capital markets.

Liberalization and the entry of private asset managers in the 1990s transformed the industry through greater product innovation, professional fund management, and stronger regulation. Over the last decade, digitalization, rising financial awareness, and increasing adoption of SIPs have accelerated retail participation and driven a structural shift of household savings from physical to financial assets. Consequently, industry AUM has witnessed exponential growth, from Rs. 10 trillion in 2014 to Rs. 81.5 trillion in 2026, establishing mutual funds as a core vehicle for long-term wealth creation.



---


Evolution of the mutual fund industry

# Classification of mutual funds

# By structure

Open-ended schemes can be purchased and redeemed on any transaction day, with no fixed maturity period. The number of units can fluctuate as the fund house sells or redeems existing units. Although a mutual fund may stop accepting new subscriptions, it must repurchase investor units at any time.

Closed-ended schemes can only be purchased during the new fund offer period and redeemed at maturity. However, they are listed on stock exchanges, allowing investors to sell units to others at a premium or discount. Interval funds allow unit purchases or sales back to the fund during specific periods.

Interval funds are mutual funds under which the units can be purchased or sold back to the fund during specific periods.

# By fund management style

Passive funds, such as exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and index funds, aim to mimic a particular index. Their efficiency is measured by tracking error, which reflects how well they replicate the index's returns. Passive funds typically have lower expenses due to lower management and operating costs.

Active funds attempt to generate higher returns than their benchmark index through active management by a fund manager. As a result, active funds have higher expenses. The key differences between passive and active funds lie in their investment approach, expense structure, and reliance on fund manager expertise.

There are five broad categories of mutual fund schemes by asset class – equity, hybrid, debt, solution-oriented, and other schemes. Each category, in turn, offers numerous funds, as shown in the tables below.

# Historical AUM growth

Robust growth in Indian mutual fund AUM

The Indian mutual fund industry has emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments within the financial services sector, driven by increasing financialization of household savings, rising retail participation, expanding SIP adoption, and growing investor preference for professionally managed investment products. This has resulted in industry QAAUM to grow at a CAGR of ~20.5% between March 2021 and March 2026, reaching Rs. 81.5 trillion as of March 2026.

The growth has been underpinned by a structural shift in savings behaviour, with retail and HNI investors accounting for 60.1% of industry AUM in March 2026 compared with 53.9% in March 2021. Additionally, monthly SIP flows have remained stable with Rs. 3,495.8 billion in fiscal 2026, showcasing greater adoption of mutual funds as a long-term wealth creation vehicle amongst individual investors. Overall, the Indian mutual fund industry is poised for continued growth, driven by its resilience and the increasing participation of individual investors.

# Mutual Fund AUM as a Percentage of Bank Deposits remains relatively low, Indicating significant growth potential

Despite the strong growth witnessed by the Indian mutual fund industry over the last decade, mutual fund Monthly Average Assets Under Management (MAAUM) continue to represent a relatively small proportion of the overall banking system deposits. While bank deposits remain the preferred savings avenue for Indian households due to their safety, liquidity, and familiarity, increasing financial awareness, rising risk appetite, and the search for inflation-beating returns have led to a gradual shift towards market-linked investment products, including mutual funds.

The gap between mutual fund assets and banking deposits highlights the substantial opportunity for further financialization of household savings in India. As investor awareness improves, disposable incomes rise, and digital investment platforms expand access to financial products, a larger share of incremental household savings is expected to be allocated towards mutual funds. This trend is further supported by growing adoption of Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs), increasing participation from Tier II and Tier III cities, and favorable demographic factors such as a young workforce and rising affluent population. Consequently, the relatively low penetration of mutual funds compared with bank deposits suggests a long-term structural growth opportunity for the industry, providing significant scope for asset accumulation over the coming years.

# Strong parentage support from SBI and Amundi

SBI, established in 1806 with over 200 years of banking experience, is India’s largest bank by advances, deposits, and branch network, with total assets of Rs. 83,215.7 billion with 23,265 branches and over 530 million customers as of March 31, 2026. SBI is ranked 45ᵗʰ in Asia by assets as of April 2026.

Amundi SA, the parent company of Amundi India Holding (Amundi India Holding together with Amundi SA, “Amundi”) is Europe’s largest asset manager headquartered in Paris, listed on Euronext Paris.

SBI Mutual Fund benefits from the combined strengths of State Bank of India, India's largest commercial bank, and Amundi SA, Europe's largest asset manager. SBI's extensive branch network, deep customer relationships, and nationwide distribution reach provides significant sourcing and cross-selling advantages, while Amundi contributes global investment expertise, product innovation capabilities, and international best practices in asset management.

# Rise of new players: Growth in India's asset management industry

While the Indian mutual fund industry continues to be led by established players, the competitive landscape has gradually diversified. The market share of the top 10 AMCs declined from 82.8% in March 2021 to 76.3% in March 2026, reflecting increased participation by niche, digital-first, and specialized fund houses. Nevertheless, scale remains a significant competitive advantage, with the top 10 players continuing to manage over three-fourths of industry assets.

Among the leading participants, bank-sponsored AMCs continue to maintain a dominant position owing to strong parentage, extensive distribution reach, customer trust, and cross-selling capabilities. In terms of QAAUM, market share of the top 3 bank led AMC has broadly remained stable despite of increase in number of fund houses in the market and increase in number of products offered by the fund houses.

The top three bank-led Asset Management Companies (AMCs) in India have consistently maintained their market leadership position, holding a stable market share of 40-41% between FY21 and FY26. This sustained dominance is attributed to their strong banking parentage, brand credibility, extensive distribution networks, and cross-selling capabilities. These factors have enabled them to deeply penetrate both Tier 1 and Tier 2/3 locations. This leadership trend is not unique to India, as top asset managers globally have also maintained their market position, driven by strong brand reputation, extensive distribution networks, and adaptability to changing market dynamics.

The top players have maintained their dominance, with the top 3 bank led AMCs holding ~40.2% share and top 5 bank led AMCs commanding over 52.1%. However, smaller AMCs are gaining traction through differentiated strategies, digital penetration, and innovation, leading to a gradual diversification of industry concentration. Bank-led AMCs continue to lead on scale and growth stability, while non-bank AMCs compete on specialization, innovation, and channel diversification, indicating a shift towards competitive depth in the industry.



---

Equity schemes have gained prominence in the last five years from 31.4% in fiscal 2021 to 43.7% in fiscal 2026. The composition of industry assets has shifted meaningfully toward equity-oriented products over the past five years. Equity schemes increased their share of industry QAAUM from 31.4% in fiscal 2021 to 43.7% in fiscal 2026, supported by strong equity market performance. Generally, equity and equity-oriented schemes have a higher fee structure compared to non-equity-oriented schemes, on account of being actively managed and hence are more profitable for AMCs.

Passive investing has also gained momentum, with passive products increasing their share from 9.5% in FY21 to 17.8% in FY26. This trend reflects rising investor awareness regarding low-cost investment products and increasing institutional participation in ETF-based strategies. The growing contribution of equity and passive products is strategically important for AMCs, as these categories generally contribute to higher operating leverage and support long-term profitability.

# State wise AUM of mutual industry of India as of March 2026

Strong AUM concentration in financial hubs; B30 and emerging states offer long term growth opportunity. As of March 2026, the top 5 states contributing to the Indian mutual fund Assets Under Management (AUM) are Maharashtra, New Delhi, Gujarat, Karnataka, and West Bengal, collectively holding 67.5% of the total mutual fund AUM. Maharashtra leads with 40.1% of the total AUM, amounting to Rs. 31,869.5 billion. The concentration of AUM in Maharashtra is attributed to strong institutional flows, the presence of major corporates, financial institutions, and a well-developed distribution ecosystem. However, increasing participation from B30 locations and emerging states with relatively lower mutual fund penetration is gradually broadening the industry's geographic footprint, which presents a significant long-term growth opportunity for AMCs.

The Indian mutual fund industry has seen a gradual rebalancing of AUM across large, medium, and small AMCs over the last few years. Large AMCs (top 3 by AUM) have maintained a stable market share of around 40.2% as of March 2026 driven by investor preference for established players. In contrast, medium-sized AMCs (next 7 players) have seen a steady decline in AUM share from 41.5% to 36.1% over from Mar-21 to Mar-26 pressure from both large AMCs and smaller players. Small AMCs have been the key beneficiaries expanding their AUM share to 29.3%, driven by rising investor acceptance of differentiated strategies, product innovation, and improved digital distribution.

# AUM distribution: Regular vs Direct - Growth trends for individual and institutional investors

Individual investors dominate the mutual fund industry. Retail participation has emerged as the primary growth driver of the Indian mutual fund industry. Individual investors accounted for 62.8% of industry AUM as of March 2026, up from 53.7% in March 2021, reflecting increasing financialization of household savings and growing adoption of mutual funds as a long-term investment vehicle. The rising contribution of retail investors has enhanced the stability and diversification of industry assets, reducing dependence on institutional flows. Continued SIP adoption, increasing financial awareness, digital onboarding, and expanding penetration across smaller cities are expected to further strengthen retail participation and support sustainable industry growth.

# Increasing share of direct sales in mutual funds

In September 2012, SEBI mandated mutual fund houses to offer products through the direct route alongside distributors, leading to the launch of direct plan offerings within existing schemes from January 2013. Direct mutual fund schemes have a lower commission ratio compared to regular schemes as they do not involve any intermediary. The share of direct plans in overall Mutual Fund AUM has increased over time, from 45.4% as of March 2021 to 49.1% as of March 2026. Despite this trend, regular plans continue to account for a majority of industry AUM, supported by first-time investors' preference for advisory-led investing, expanding distributor networks, and growing participation from smaller cities. Accordingly, both direct and intermediary-led channels are expected to remain important drivers of industry growth over the medium term. Going forward, we expect further growth in direct plan AUMs with increasing investor awareness and integration of user interfaces through digital channels.

# T30-B30 analysis of mutual fund monthly average AUM: B30 locations have emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of the mutual fund industry

The monthly average Assets Under Management (AUMs) in top 30 (T30) cities far exceed those in the top 30 (B30) cities. As of March 2026, T30 cities had Rs 65.0 trillion in AUM, compared to Rs 14.4 trillion in B30 cities. However, B30 locations have emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of the mutual fund industry, with MAAUM growing at a CAGR of 22.5% between March 2021 and March 2026, compared with 19.3% for T30 cities.

The share of B30 assets increased from 16.3% in March 2021 to 18.2% in March 2026, reflecting improving financial awareness, greater digital penetration, and expansion of distribution networks beyond metropolitan markets. Despite this growth, B30 cities account for less than one-fifth of industry assets, indicating significant untapped potential. Increasing penetration in these markets is expected to remain a key driver of incremental industry growth over the medium term.

# Vintage of mutual fund AUM

The increasing share of long-tenure equity assets highlights improving investor maturity and growing preference for long-term wealth creation through mutual funds. As of March 2026, equity schemes with a vintage exceeding 24 months accounted for approximately Rs. 21.6 trillion AUM, significantly higher than comparable levels in earlier periods.

The increasing proportion of seasoned equity assets reflects greater investor confidence in mutual funds as a long-term savings and investment vehicle. Further, longer holding periods enhance revenue visibility and fee persistence for asset managers while reducing redemption volatility.

# Headroom exists for Indian mutual fund industry to grow

India's mutual fund AUM-to-GDP ratio increased from 16.2% in March 2021 to 23.2% in March 2026, reflecting accelerating financialization of savings and increasing participation in capital markets.

However, mutual fund penetration remains significantly lower than developed markets such as the United States, Canada, and France, where AUM-to-GDP ratios exceed 80%. This gap highlights the substantial long-term growth potential for India's asset management industry. Crisil believes that supported by rising incomes, growing financial literacy, increasing retirement savings needs, and expanding digital distribution, India is expected to witness continued growth in mutual fund penetration over the coming years, thereby opening a large revenue pool potential for AMCs.

# Impact of market volatility on equity mutual fund inflows

During fiscal 2026, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) have exhibited volatility amidst global uncertainty, with significant net outflows, particularly in March 2026 (Rs. 1,177.8 billion), due to global risk aversion. However, Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) and Mutual Funds (MFs) have maintained consistent net inflows, with DIIs peaking at Rs. 1,429.6 billion in March 2026 and MFs supported by steady SIP contributions, effectively offsetting FII outflows and reinforcing stability in India's equity market.

Passive funds have risen steadily over a small base. In India, passive investing has been gaining traction for several years, as reflected in the significant increase in assets under management (AUM). As awareness about passive investing continues to grow, financial advisors are increasingly recommending these funds to their clients. Additionally, high net worth individuals (HNIs) and family offices are also shifting their investments towards passive funds, drawn by their cost-effectiveness and the inconsistent performance of actively managed funds. Passive Funds QAAUM for the March 2026 stood at Rs. 14,515.4 billion with total share of Passive Funds to Total AUM is around 17.8%.
